1 | P a g e  
 
 
June 15, 2026 
 
 
Dr. Mehmet Oz, Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
Attn: CMS-0062-P 
Mail Stop C4-26-05 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
 
Submitted Electronically: http://www.regulations.gov  
Re: Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
 
UnitedHealth Group (UHG) is pleased to submit comments to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid 
Services (CMS) regarding the Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule 
(the “Proposed Rule”). The Proposed Rule was published in the Federal Register on April 14, 2026 (91 FR 
19890) and would implement new standards and requirements that govern electronic prior authorization 
for all drugs across Medicare Advantage, Medicaid/CHIP, and Qualified Health Plans (QHPs) offered 
through the Federally Facilitated Exchanges (FFEs).  
 
UHG’s mission is to help people live healthier lives and make the health care system work better for 
everyone. Through UnitedHealthcare (UHC), our health benefits business, and Optum, our health 
services business, we work with employers, providers, and governments to serve people and execute on 
our vision for a value-based system of care that provides affordable health care, improves outcomes, 
lessens the burden of disease, and promotes a healthier lifestyle. 
 
UHG is supportive of CMS’s continued work on driving toward an interoperable health system, including 
its current effort to streamline and standardize electronic prior authorization for all drugs. Doing so will 
enable more patients to access medically necessary drugs sooner, overall improving health outcomes, 
patient experience, and administrative burden for providers. Given the current complexities present 
across the various stakeholders involved in building an interoperable health care system, we believe a 
nuanced approach is required and should account for the current state of health care technology 
implementation as well as the realities of technology deployment at scale. Our comments on the 
proposed rule below are therefore intended to assist in this process as we work with CMS and others 
within the health care community to advance the adoption of interoperable data systems. We also 
provide feedback on several of the requests for information (RFIs) CMS included at the end of its 
proposed rule to offer further support and feedback on future policy directions.  
 
 
 
2 
 
General Comments 
 
Requiring Unexpired Versions of NCPDP Standards 
 
CMS proposes to require that state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, 
CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs support an unexpired version of the NCPDP 
SCRIPT, Formulary and Benefit (F&B), and Real Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) standard. Doing so 
would support electronic prior authorization of drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit, make formulary 
and benefits information available, and enable the exchange of real-time coverage information for such 
drugs.  
 
Overall, UHG is supportive of CMS’s proposal to require impacted payers to support unexpired versions 
of NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB. Generally, these standards are widely adopted and used within the 
industry to support drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit. Additionally, all three standards are 
federally mandated standards for their respective functions under Medicare Part D at 42 CFR 423.160, 
and so adopting them here would establish consistent, unified standards across pharmacy benefit 
transactions regardless of plan type. This would serve to reduce implementation burden for prescribers 
and payers who participate in multiple programs such as Medicare Part D and state Medicaid programs. 
 
UHG supports the proposed requirement for impacted payers to support unexpired versions of the 
NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB standards. 
 
Other Existing Technical Solutions 
 
As part of its proposal to require impacted payers to support unexpired versions of the NCPDP 
standards, CMS asked whether there are other existing technical solutions or methods that impacted 
payers could utilize to indicate to providers how a prior authorization request for a drug should be 
submitted. 
 
While there are existing technical solutions that impacted payers can utilize, we believe that there is not 
a single, one-source solution currently available. In general, the NCPDP F&B and RTPB standards are 
able to provide information on drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit. They can also communicate 
whether a drug that is not covered under the pharmacy benefit may be covered under the medical benefit 
instead. However, these tools may not have full visibility into drug coverage under a medical benefit and 
so may be limited in their ability to determine definitively whether a drug is covered under such medical 
benefit. The same is true in the reverse from the medical benefit side. In 2025, CAQH CORE published 
guidance about using the X12 270/271 transaction set to support the exchange of information for drugs 
covered under the medical benefit; however, this would not have access to information for drugs 
covered under the pharmacy benefit. As such, there is no single tool currently available with access to 
both pharmacy and medical benefit to make the appropriate designation of coverage, but all tools can 
work in tandem to provide this information. 
 
UHG recommends that CMS account for the current state of technical capabilities by supporting 
multi-standard approaches that allow impacted payers to leverage existing tools in tandem to 
determine appropriate prior authorization pathways. 
 
3 
 
Use Existing Connectivity and Network Approaches to Support Scalable Implementation 
 
CMS proposes separate standards pathways for electronic prior authorization of drugs depending on 
whether the drug is covered under the medical benefit or pharmacy benefit. Under the proposal, 
impacted payers would use FHIR-based Prior Authorization API standards for drugs covered under a 
medical benefit, while impacted payers other than Medicare Advantage organizations would support 
NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB standards for drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit. CMS further 
states that the Prior Authorization API can be used to support drugs under a medical benefit, but should 
not be used for prior authorization of drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit. 
 
UHG supports CMS’s effort to align standards with the benefit pathway through which a drug is covered. 
At the same time, operational experience suggests that drug authorization workflows may require 
scalable approaches for determining the appropriate pathway and accessing the data elements needed 
to evaluate clinical criteria, particularly where relevant clinical information resides in provider or health 
system environments. 
 
UHG encourages CMS to consider how these capabilities can be implemented to accurately access 
clinical data to process prior authorizations at scale. While payers and pharmacy benefit managers can 
establish FHIR connectivity with individual health systems, doing so through one-to-one integrations may 
require separate contracting, technical implementation, testing, and ongoing maintenance for each 
health system connection. In contrast, existing NCPDP connectivity already supports data exchange with 
individual health systems today. This approach could materially slow adoption and make it difficult to 
achieve the level of automation and workflow integration that CMS intends to promote. 
 
To support scalable implementation, UHG believes CMS should consider approaches that allow payers 
and pharmacy benefit managers to leverage CMS-aligned networks such as TEFCA for the prior 
authorization use case. While TEFCA participants are not currently required to respond to inquiries for 
payment and operations, which include pharmacy benefit manager prior authorization, requiring TEFCA 
participants to respond with clinical data for prior authorization would make data available at scale. This 
would further obviate the need to outreach to providers separately and support unique connections, 
which would be duplicative to the data infrastructure supporting treatment use cases today. We believe 
this approach would allow stakeholders to access the data elements needed to evaluate clinical criteria 
for the requested drug at scale, while avoiding the complexity and time associated with establishing 
individualized connections with each health system. This would support CMS’s goals of improving 
automation, reducing administrative burden, and enabling a more consistent provider experience across 
the market, while preserving the separate standards pathways CMS has proposed for medical-benefit 
and pharmacy-benefit drug prior authorization. 
 
UHG recommends that CMS consider approaches to enable scalable data exchange for prior 
authorization—including through TEFCA and existing NCPDP connectivity—to reduce duplicative 
provider burden and support implementation at scale. 
 
October 1, 2027 Compliance Date 
 
A majority of the core provisions in CMS’s proposed rule have a proposed effective date of October 1, 
2027, including the proposed requirements on impacted payers to support unexpired versions of the 
4 
 
NCPDP standards, the requirement on impacted payers to expand the scope of the required FHIR Prior 
Authorization API to incorporate drugs covered under a medical benefit, and many of the new prior 
authorization decision timeframes for prescription drugs, among other proposed changes.  
 
UHG strongly supports CMS’s goal of advancing a more connected, patient-centered digital health 
ecosystem and remains committed to industry efforts to accelerate adoption of Fast Healthcare 
Interoperability Resources (FHIR)-based standards and electronic prior authorization workflows. 
Consistent with that commitment, we are actively engaging with partners across the health care 
ecosystem to enable real-world data exchange that improves both provider and patient experience. 
Through these efforts, we have observed that achieving the outcomes envisioned by both industry 
initiatives and this proposed rule—particularly seamless, end-to-end workflow integration across 
payers, providers, and electronic health record systems—requires coordinated readiness across 
multiple stakeholders and technology environments. 
 
In that context, UHG recommends that CMS consider an implementation timeline of up to 24 months 
following publication of the final rule to support scalable and durable implementation. This approach 
would help ensure that required capabilities are not only deployed, but fully operationalized across 
trading partners, reducing the risk of fragmented or partial adoption that could undermine CMS’s 
intended outcomes. Calibrating the timeline in this manner would not slow progress; rather, it would 
increase the likelihood of meaningful, sustained interoperability consistent with the goals of both the 
proposed rule and broader interoperability efforts. 
 
UHG recommends extending the implementation timeline of up to 24 months following publication 
of the final rule. 
 
Reporting Deadlines for Publicly Reported Prior Authorization Metrics 
 
CMS proposes to modify the deadlines for Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care 
entities to report certain metrics about prior authorizations for drugs, as well as for non-drug items and 
services, to be no later than 90 days after the end of their contract rating period. 
 
UHG respectfully urges CMS to retain the existing uniform March 31 annual deadline for all impacted 
payers for the public posting of prior authorization metrics and for reporting Patient Access API usage 
metrics, rather than adopting the proposed requirement that states require Medicaid managed care 
plans and CHIP managed care entities to report prior authorization metrics for both drugs and non-drug 
items and services within 90 days of the close of each state’s contract rating period. While UHG 
understands CMS’s rationale for aligning Medicaid/CHIP managed care reporting timelines with state-
specific contract rating periods, replacing a single, uniform federal deadline with multiple state-specific 
deadlines for Medicaid/CHIP managed care plans would introduce unnecessary complexity into the 
reporting process and, more importantly, undermine the meaningful comparison of prior authorization 
metrics across payers and programs. 
  
Fragmenting reporting timelines by state contract rating period would result in data being published at 
different times and based on different reference periods, reducing transparency and comparability for 
beneficiaries and other stakeholders. By contrast, uniform calendar year reporting with a consistent 
March 31 deadline would better serve Medicaid beneficiaries by producing easy-to-understand, 
5 
 
comparable metrics without requiring reconciliation of disparate state-specific reporting windows. 
Maintaining a single March 31 deadline would also promote standardized reporting across all impacted 
payer types. 
 
UHG recommends retaining the March 31 annual deadline for Medicaid/CHIP managed care 
entities to publicly report prior authorization metrics. 
 
Endpoint Reporting 
 
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to report all API endpoints to CMS, in the form of an Endpoint 
Resource, as defined by an unexpired version of the FHIR standard adopted in 45 CFR 170.215(a), 
including, if multiple, appropriate use cases for each. 
 
UHG supports CMS’s goal of improving the discoverability and accessibility of payer API endpoints, and 
we appreciate the intent behind establishing a centralized directory to facilitate more efficient 
interoperability. Based on our operational experience, we believe there may be an opportunity to further 
enhance the effectiveness of such a directory by accounting for the complexity of how payer endpoints 
are structured in practice. For example, a single payer organization may maintain multiple endpoints for 
the same API function across different plans, products, benefit structures, and delegated vendor 
arrangements. In particular, prior authorization workflows may involve multiple internal systems and 
external partners depending on the service type, benefit design, or drug authorization pathway. As a 
result, a directory may need to support a more hierarchical and flexible structure that allows multiple 
endpoints to be mapped to a single payer entity, including distinctions at the plan level and for specific 
use cases. 
 
In addition, while a centralized directory can improve transparency and help stakeholders identify 
available endpoints, additional considerations may be needed to ensure that it supports seamless 
integration at scale. Specifically, stakeholders will still need to establish and maintain the technical, 
security, and workflow connections required to use each endpoint. UHG believes that pairing endpoint 
transparency with complementary strategies that support more scalable connectivity (e.g., network-
based approaches or standardized integration pathways) could further advance CMS’s goals of reducing 
administrative burden and improving interoperability. 
 
UHG supports a public repository of payer API endpoints but recommends it account for the 
complexity of how payer endpoints are structured in practice.  
 
Modifications to HIPAA Standards Related to Prior Authorization 
 
In this rule, CMS proposes to modify the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) 
Administrative Simplification transaction standards to adopt FHIR-based standards for prior 
authorization and related transactions. As part of this approach, CMS proposes to apply the FHIR 
standards described in this rule to all “referral certification and authorization transactions” defined at 45 
CFR 162.1301, which would extend beyond the impacted payers subject to the interoperability and prior 
authorization requirements and apply to all covered entities under HIPAA. CMS also proposes to 
integrate the Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD) implementation specification into the prior 
authorization workflow to support earlier identification of prior authorization requirements. In addition, 
6 
 
CMS seeks to align these FHIR-based capabilities with existing administrative transactions, including 
those related to eligibility inquiries, to facilitate more streamlined and automated prior authorization 
processes across the health care system. Finally, as part of its corresponding requests for information, 
CMS asks whether it should adopt any later versions of the proposed standards, including more recent 
versions that are currently available and versions that may become available between the publication of 
the proposed and final rules. We respond to each of these elements of the proposed modifications to 
HIPAA standards related to prior authorization in turn.  
 
Adopting FHIR Standards for All “Referral Certification and Authorization Transactions” 
 
UHG appreciates CMS’s efforts to modernize administrative transactions and advance a more 
interoperable, standards-based prior authorization environment across the health care system. We 
support the broader goal of moving toward FHIR-based workflows where those standards can improve 
efficiency, reduce provider burden, and better align with evolving digital processes. CMS’s proposal to 
adopt FHIR standards for prior authorization-related transactions reflects an important step in that 
direction.  
 
At the same time, UHG believes there is an opportunity to further refine this proposal to support a more 
orderly transition for covered entities and to avoid unnecessary disruption to workflows that are currently 
functioning effectively. In particular, CMS’s alternative proposal would apply the FHIR standards of the 
proposed rule to all “referral certification and authorization transactions” described in 45 CFR 162.1301. 
As a practical matter, referral transactions today are already processed at significant scale using the X12 
278 transaction standard, and these transactions continue to serve important operational needs across 
the industry. By contrast, FHIR-based referral workflows have not yet been tested or implemented at 
comparable scale. For that reason, UHG encourages CMS not to modify the standard being used for 
referrals without first pursuing pilot testing or phased adoption. This would be more consistent with the 
historical approach used to introduce new HIPAA transaction standards and would help preserve 
business continuity while implementation experience matures.  
 
Adopting FHIR Standards for Eligibility Determinations 
 
UHG also appreciates CMS’s efforts to improve transparency and enable earlier identification of prior 
authorization requirements within clinical and administrative workflows. We agree that supporting 
providers in understanding, at an earlier stage, whether prior authorization may be required has the 
potential to reduce downstream burden and improve efficiency. At the same time, UHG believes the 
proposal could be strengthened by more clearly distinguishing these capabilities from the existing HIPAA 
“eligibility for a health plan” transaction defined at 45 CFR 162.1201. As currently defined, that 
transaction is intended to support inquiries regarding eligibility, coverage, and benefits associated with a 
health plan, and does not expressly include determinations related to prior authorization requirements. 
 
From an implementation perspective, UHG believes additional clarity would be helpful where the 
proposed framework differentiates transaction standards based on the intent of the inquiry. In practice, 
that distinction may not always be clear at the time a transaction is initiated. For example, when a 
provider or scheduling system checks a patient’s coverage during appointment scheduling, it may be 
difficult to determine whether the inquiry is solely an eligibility verification or part of a prior authorization 
determination. This dynamic may be particularly relevant for ancillary services—such as physical 
7 
 
therapy, long-term care, and similar services—where clinical and utilization management considerations 
may not yet be fully developed at the time of scheduling. Providing additional guidance on how to 
consistently apply the appropriate standard in these scenarios could help reduce ambiguity for covered 
entities and technology vendors and support more consistent compliance with HIPAA Administrative 
Simplification requirements. 
 
To support CMS’s objectives while minimizing operational complexity, UHG strongly recommends CMS 
consider alternative approaches that preserve clear boundaries between existing transaction types. For 
example, integrating prior-authorization-related discovery functionality within the referral certification 
and authorization transaction framework may provide a more intuitive implementation pathway, as 
those transactions represent the initial steps in the prior authorization process under 45 CFR 162.1301. 
Alternatively, CMS could consider establishing a distinct transaction type for determining whether prior 
authorization is required and specifying the applicable FHIR standard for that function. Either approach 
could help advance CMS’s goals while maintaining clarity in how transaction standards are applied 
across workflows. 
 
More broadly, UHG encourages CMS to continue aligning policy design with real-world workflow timing 
and system capabilities to ensure successful implementation. Clarifying transaction boundaries and 
sequencing the transition in a manner that reflects current industry practices would help reduce 
confusion for providers and technology developers, preserve functioning processes, and support 
broader adoption of FHIR-based prior authorization capabilities over time. 
 
Adopting Later Versions of Proposed Standards 
 
As stated, CMS asks whether it should adopt any later versions of the proposed standards, including 
more recent versions that are currently available and versions that may become available between the 
publication of the proposed and final rules. Overall, UHG supports CMS's current approach with the 
NCPDP standards outlined in the proposed rule. We further recommend, however, that CMS not adopt 
other versions of NCPDP standards beyond those proposed in this rule—or, more specifically, that the 
final rule name no version newer than NCPDP SCRIPT Standard Version 2023011 (as codified at 45 CFR 
170.205(b)), NCPDP Formulary & Benefit Standard Version 60 (as codified at 45 CFR 170.205(u)), and 
NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit Standard Version 13 (as codified at 45 CFR 170.205(c)).  
 
The industry is in active transition to the currently proposed versions. Thus, stakeholders are largely not 
prepared for a subsequent version mandate. The standards named in this proposed rule were finalized 
for Part D purposes in the Medicare Part D e-prescribing standards final rule in June 2024, with 
compliance dates of January 1, 2027 (F&B v60, RTPB v13) and January 1, 2028 (SCRIPT 2023011). 
Industry stakeholders—including health IT developers, pharmacies, pharmacy benefit managers, payers, 
and network intermediaries—are currently mid-implementation of these transitions. The Part D 
compliance deadlines are imminent, and the impacted payers newly brought into scope under CMS-
0062-P (Medicaid, CHIP, and QHP issuers) are in implementation phases. Requiring a newer version of 
any of these three standards in the final rule would effectively render ongoing implementation work 
obsolete and impose significant additional development, testing, and deployment costs on entities that 
have already committed resources to the currently named versions. Naming versions other than those 
listed in the proposed rule would also create a misalignment with the regulations listed above, causing 
confusion for the industry. 
8 
 
 
UHG recommends that CMS pursue a phased and clearly delineated transition to FHIR-based prior 
authorization standards, preserve existing transaction frameworks where operationally effective, 
maintain clear boundaries between transaction types, and avoid adopting NCPDP standard 
versions newer than those proposed in this rule. 
 
Thank you for your thoughtful consideration of our comments. As stated, UHG is committed to working 
with CMS and other stakeholders to ensure the health care system advances toward a more modern and 
technology-enabled approach. Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
CEO, Optum Insight 
 
 
9 
 
Request for Information (RFI) Responses 
 
Re: B. Request for Information: Increasing Health Care Resiliency 
UnitedHealth Group (UHG) appreciates the opportunity to provide feedback on the Centers for Medicare 
& Medicaid Services’ (CMS) Request for Information (RFI): Increasing Health Care Resiliency and CMS’ 
commitment to enhancing the health care system’s resilience against cyber threats. CMS’ RFI comes at 
a crucial time for the country’s health care system. Cyber threats are increasing in frequency, 
sophistication, and operational impact, including AI-enabled capabilities. UHG and other health care 
companies are facing growing challenges to protect patients’ data, ensure care continuity, and maintain 
vital health care services. We urge CMS to adopt voluntary, flexible, and risk-based cybersecurity 
approaches that advance preparedness across the health sector while accounting for the diverse 
operational, technical, and financial capabilities of the health care entities involved. 
UHG appreciates CMS’ leadership in soliciting stakeholder feedback on these critical issues, and we 
welcome the opportunity to share our recommendations to support a more resilient, secure, and 
coordinated health care system. Please see below for UHG responses and recommendations to specific 
questions outlined in this RFI. 
How have existing statutes and regulations, within CMS' purview, shaped your cybersecurity 
strategies, and what changes or additions by CMS would enhance your ability to safeguard health 
information? 
As CMS considers new changes or additions to statutes and regulations, within its purview, seeking to 
safeguard health information, UHG recommends avoiding any new mandates and regulations that 
increase compliance costs but do not provide commensurate benefits for cybersecurity interests. Any 
new cybersecurity requirements should build off of and grant reciprocity to existing cybersecurity 
compliance frameworks. Specifically, we recommend the following: 
Re-authorize Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act (CISA) of 2015. CMS should coordinate with HHS 
to advocate that Congress re-authorize the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 for no less 
than a 10-year period to enhance private entities’ protection of data, devices, and networks while 
promoting continuity for cyber threat information sharing between industry and government partners 
within a secure policy and legal framework. 
Establish minimum cyber standards for the health sector. CMS should work collaboratively with 
Congress, the private sector, and other federal agencies with health-sector jurisdiction, to establish 
mandatory minimum cybersecurity standards for health entities. UHG recommends accompanying 
financial and technical support for Medicare and Medicaid providers, particularly for small, rural and 
safety net providers with standards development and implementation. An example approach would be 
an incentive-based pilot program for entities who provide evidence from an independent third-party 
auditor of the adoption of cybersecurity practices aligned with the National Institute of Standards and 
Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 and Section 405(d) of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015. 
10 
 
Harmonize instead of duplicate. CMS should prioritize harmonization of its requirements with existing 
frameworks (e.g., Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), Health Information Trust 
Alliance (HITRUST), and NIST) rather than introducing new or duplicative mandates that increase 
complexity without improving security outcomes. CMS should provide a formal crosswalk of controls to 
clarify how its requirements align with existing frameworks. 
Embed security-by-design into interoperability requirements. CMS should embed security-by-design 
into all interoperability requirements, ensuring that authentication, authorization, encryption, and 
monitoring controls are inherent to Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)/Application 
Programming Interface (API)-based data exchange rather than applied after implementation.   
Streamline reporting. CMS should reduce duplicative and high-risk reporting requirements by allowing 
third-party attestation letters, standardized control mappings, and summary-level documentation in 
place of detailed security artifacts that increase exposure risk. This approach reduces compliance 
burden while protecting sensitive security information. 
Provide regulatory consistency. CMS should establish clear and consistent regulatory expectations 
across CMS, the Office for Civil Rights (OCR), and state entities to eliminate conflicting interpretations.  
Advance platform-based interoperability. CMS should advance platform-based interoperability 
models (e.g., enterprise FHIR frameworks) that promote reuse, scalability, and centralized security 
controls rather than fragmented, point-to-point implementations.   
Enforce “minimum necessary” data sharing. CMS should seek to balance interoperability with 
cybersecurity risk by enforcing “minimum necessary” data sharing principles and ensuring that 
increased data access does not outpace the maturity of security controls. 
Incorporate identity proofing for ePA. CMS should incorporate provider and delegate identity (ID) 
proofing as a condition of API access before CMS-0062-P is finalized to close this security gap, 
consistent with NIST SP 800-63-4 digital ID guidelines. This action will help protect against cyberattacks 
and strengthen the overall network.  
What are the major challenges and barriers that health care organizations face in implementing 
robust cybersecurity measures? How have health care organizations overcome these challenges 
and barriers? 
Below we highlight overarching, key challenges facing the health care ecosystem as entities and the 
government look to partner to develop a more robust health care system that is better poised to prevent 
cybersecurity breaches and respond swiftly in the case of attacks. Examples include:  
Numerous competing standards. One main issue facing health care companies related to 
cybersecurity is the plethora of competing standards in this space. Entities are subject to many different 
and potentially conflicting regulations and contractual obligations.  These numerous requirements can 
pose operational and administrative challenges and necessitate significant time and resource 
consumption. Any new guidance should align with existing, widely adopted frameworks to reduce 
administrative burden and unnecessary complexity for stakeholders.  
11 
 
Balance between data availability and security. Providing consumers with greater access to their 
health data is an important goal; however, the expansion of access increases the amount of security 
needed as it makes the cyberattack surface larger. Therefore, we recommend CMS evaluates 
appropriate security needs as access to new or additional data increases.    
Balance between detailed reporting and data protection. The more detailed security information 
health care entities must provide to CMS and its state partners, the more risk exists that the information 
can be accessed and exploited. Proxies for this type of detailed security information should be 
encouraged.  
What are the most effective current practices, technologies, and innovative strategies for 
preventing, detecting, and responding to cyberattacks in the health care sector? Should CMS 
propose any of these practices or strategies as regulatory requirements within its purview?  
UHG supports efforts to strengthen our national cybersecurity infrastructure, including greater 
coordination of notification to law enforcement while standardizing and modernizing federal 
cybersecurity incident reporting. Today, there are disparate breach notification reporting requirements 
involving multiple federal agencies (e.g., OCR, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the 
Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and states). Establishing streamlined and 
coordinated reporting requirements can ensure robust and timely reporting touches a broad range of 
stakeholders, without causing undue burden on entities experiencing an incident. 
Since time is of the essence in containing a cyber incident, entities should report cybersecurity incidents 
as soon as possible but be allowed a minimum of 72 hours after an incident is confirmed to report, 
allowing the entity to focus first on immediate steps to stop or mitigate the incident, and only then on 
collecting and collating the information necessary to file a report. Thereafter, adequate time should be 
provided to support system restoration. Finally, efforts should be made to avoid duplicative, multiple, or 
inconsistent reporting. Harmonizing reporting requirements so each entity is required to report a specific 
incident only once and to a single government agency will streamline the reporting process, avoid double 
counting, and allow both affected entities and government agencies to utilize their resources more 
efficiently. Importantly, cyber incident reporting should be limited to material incidents that have the 
potential to cause harm to critical infrastructure and should not be required for “potential” or 
“suspected” incidents. 
How do the enrollment and implementation processes for health care clearinghouses affect the 
health care industry’s ability to remain resilient? How could this be improved? 
The largest enrollment issues are with state Medicaid agencies and CMS Medicare/HIPAA Eligibility 
Transaction System (HETS). Clearinghouses have worked closely with commercial payers, Medicare 
Advantage plans, and Managed Care Organizations to streamline provider enrollment, but issues with 
the state and federal-run gateways continue to persist. Within state Medicaid agencies, the biggest 
hurdle is the state gateway not allowing the transfer of provider enrollments from one Trading Partner ID 
(TPID) to another, even if owned by the same organization, without the provider having to completely re-
attest. This makes it difficult to move providers between clearinghouses, or even between different 
platforms within the same clearinghouse organization, creating significant work for providers.  
12 
 
Additionally, CMS recently removed trading partner access to the HETS validation, preventing 
clearinghouses without a direct connection from using approved intermediary relationships to validate 
that a National Provider Identifier (NPI) is correctly associated with a TPID. This change requires 
providers to go into the HETS tool and validate information, and make their own updates, significantly 
increasing provider burden. Since this change, multiple provider organizations have been unable to 
submit claims because they are unclear about the new processes and why their clearinghouse cannot 
provide the previous level of support.  
CMS should promote greater portability of provider enrollment records across trading partner 
relationships and evaluate mechanisms for authorized clearinghouses to support HETS validation 
activities. These changes would reduce provider burden and improve industry resilience by enabling 
providers and clearinghouses to adapt more quickly to operational disruptions, platform migrations, or 
changes in clearinghouse relationships. 
What are the potential benefits and challenges of a health care system with more point-to-point 
connections? 
Expanding point-to-point connections would present significant security and operational challenges for 
the health sector. More direct connections mean a substantially larger number of system endpoints to 
secure, making it considerably more difficult to monitor access rights, usage patterns, and potentially 
unauthorized activity across the entire network. Much of the specialized work currently performed by 
clearinghouses, transaction validation, translation, and routing would shift to the payer and provider 
systems that originate and receive transactions. Rather than simplifying the ecosystem by removing an 
intermediary, this approach would likely generate greater complexity, cost, and risk for all entities 
involved.  
While point-to-point connections can function effectively within a limited scope for specific, defined 
purposes, they are not capable of scaling nationwide to support seamless exchange between the 
thousands of providers and plans within the U.S. health system. This issue persists even with the 
adoption of FHIR APIs. FHIR does not eliminate the underlying structural challenge.  
Instead, clearinghouses and health information networks address specific, persistent barriers to scaling 
point-to-point transactions: 1) not all providers can natively generate compliant transactions; 2) not all 
payers accept transactions identically, as payers retain latitude to create companion guides requiring 
variations from standards, including FHIR; and 3) translation, validation, and routing remain necessary 
functions regardless of which standard is in use. FHIR itself allows for significant variation in individual 
organization API implementations, making it no more uniformly standardized in practice than X12 or 
Consolidated Clinical Document Architecture (C-CDA). Compounding this further, payers maintain 
multiple endpoints organized by plan, and prior authorization alone may involve multiple authorization 
processing partners, making the issue more complex, not less. 
 
 
 
 
13 
 
What role do health care clearinghouses play in supporting point-to-point connections, and what 
role do they play in supporting the exchange of health care data? 
Clearinghouses support a contractual structure that is point-to-point (e.g., bilateral agreements between 
a provider and a payer) while supporting a technical structure that is networked.  This hybrid approach 
supports nationwide interoperability by preserving existing contractual relationships while enabling more 
efficient and scalable transaction exchange. Payers and providers do not have disputes regarding data 
use rights because they are narrowly constrained in the bilateral agreements, and at the same time they 
have a single point of connection to reach all of the providers or payers they need to connect to, without 
having to modify their transaction formats to meet each connection’s requirements. This significantly 
reduces cost and speeds up implementation timelines for the industry. Clearinghouses recognize the 
value of real-time transactions, with many clearinghouses already offering JavaScript Object Notation 
(JSON) APIs for eligibility and claim status, and most clearinghouses are embracing FHIR for prior 
authorization transactions.   
To ensure clearinghouses can continue to transact with each other utilizing FHIR, the Cooperative 
Exchange recently launched the Trebuchet Pilot Cohort for clearinghouse-to-clearinghouse prior 
authorization transactions. This initiative ensures that network capacity can expand to clearinghouse-to-
clearinghouse exchange, ensuring providers and payers do not have to build point-to-point connections 
or join multiple clearinghouses. 
What options are available or recommended for streamlining transition processes, including 
moving from one health care clearinghouse to another, when one is impacted by a cyberattack? 
One of the main issues with switching between clearinghouses is exclusivity terms and lock-ins within 
contracts. Should providers or payers need to switch clearinghouses unexpectedly and rapidly, such 
clauses would be problematic, therefore we recommend that clearinghouses exclude such terms from 
contracts.  
 
Re: C. Request for Information: Improving Implementation of Payer Application Programming 
Interface Technology 
UnitedHealth Group (UHG) appreciates the opportunity to provide feedback on the Centers for Medicare 
& Medicaid Services (CMS) Request for Information (RFI): Improving Implementation of Payer Application 
Programming Interface Technology. UHG supports CMS’ goals of advancing a more connected and 
patient-centered health care system through interoperable and standards-based data exchange. There 
is significant potential for application programming interfaces (APIs) to improve health information 
access, enhance coordination of care, and minimize administrative burden while empowering providers 
and patients with actionable and timely health care data. As CMS and other policymakers consider 
future enhancements to payer API technology, focus should be given to not only expanding data 
availability in a secure fashion but also ways to improve the quality, reliability, usability, and consistency 
of data across payers. We greatly appreciate being able to share our recommendations to help 
strengthen payer API technology implementation and maximize value for patients, payers, providers, as 
well as other health care stakeholders. 
14 
 
Overall, UHG is aligned with CMS’ interoperability goals and is actively advancing electronic prior 
authorization at scale today. To ensure successful implementation of payer APIs, CMS should: 
Focus on outcomes over compliance. Success should be measured by metrics such as automation 
rates, provider burden reduction, and time to therapy. 
Prioritize data liquidity. We recommend expanding frameworks (e.g., Trusted Exchange Framework and 
Common Agreement (TEFCA)) to support pharmacy prior authorization use cases and structured clinical 
data exchange. 
Preserve and align with existing pharmacy infrastructure. We support maintaining National Council 
for Prescription Drug Programs’ (NCPDP) standards and avoiding disruption to highly adopted pharmacy 
workflows. 
Require end-to-end interoperability testing. UHG supports validating real-world workflows, not only 
API endpoints.   
Please see below for UHG responses and recommendations to specific questions outlined in this RFI. 
What aspects of API implementation pose the most significant implementation difficulties, and 
where do commenters perceive the potential for lack of conformance with the API technical 
requirements? 
Supporting multiple versions of the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) implementation 
guides simultaneously has been challenging when newer versions are not all backward compatible. 
Coalescing to a single version and giving the industry time to adopt it would be helpful in addressing this 
challenge. FHIR standards are advancing at a rapid pace, and a more measured release cadence would 
enable broader implementation across the industry. This approach, in turn, would lead to better 
feedback and improved future versions. Additionally, even where implementation guides are mature and 
widely adopted, standards necessarily allow for implementation discretion, resulting in variation across 
organizations and systems. FHIR APIs are not “plug and play”. Although the security frameworks 
surrounding FHIR APIs are well-developed, establishing secure point-to-point connectivity requires 
substantial implementation effort by both parties. 
What value would the certification of payer API technology provide to payers, providers, and 
patients? What would be the benefits and burdens of requiring certification of payer API technology 
for payers, providers, and patients?  
As has been demonstrated with the current certification program for APIs for provider systems, 
certification does not equate to real-world performance. Despite having certification criteria for FHIR 
APIs for years, connecting to an EHR requires the same amount of work as without certification. 
Certification does not reduce implementation burden, and it increases cost for the entire industry. In 
contrast, CMS National Standards Group (NSG) performs real-world audits on Health Insurance 
Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) transactions to ensure compliance. The work effort for these 
on-the-spot audits is significantly lower, while also demonstrating that the standards are being followed 
in practice, not just for a one-time certification. We believe this type of auditing would be more beneficial 
for providers, patients, and payers than a certification program. 
15 
 
However, if CMS chooses to move forward with payer API certification in the future, we recommend that 
it be implemented in a pragmatic, use-case-driven manner. Continued collaboration between CMS, the 
Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC), and industry stakeholders 
will be important to ensure certification remains scalable, effective, and not unnecessarily burdensome.  
Payer API (health IT) certification is directionally aligned with the broader goal of improving consistency 
and predictability in interoperability across payers, providers, and vendors. A well-defined certification 
approach can help establish confidence that APIs are compliant, function as intended, and are capable 
of supporting real-world data exchange at scale. 
At the same time, the approach to certification will be critical. If implemented in an overly prescriptive 
manner, there is a risk of introducing incremental cost and operational overhead without delivering 
proportional improvements in interoperability outcomes. Certification should therefore be right-sized 
and focused on the specific payer use cases and API capabilities that are central to achieving the policy 
intent, rather than requiring broad alignment to requirements that may not be directly applicable.  
Certification should prioritize the core set of capabilities that will drive the majority of real-world 
transactions. Attempting to certify against every edge case or low-frequency scenario is likely to increase 
complexity without materially improving outcomes. A more pragmatic approach would focus on the 
highest-impact workflows, while allowing less common scenarios to mature over time through 
implementation experience. 
A more targeted certification construct (for example, a payer-focused data set aligned to key 
interoperability use cases) could help strike the right balance between advancing interoperability and 
maintaining implementation feasibility. This approach would allow organizations to focus on what is 
most relevant to payer workflows, while still supporting meaningful progress toward standardized data 
exchange.  
Certification can also play a valuable role in enabling vendors and partners to demonstrate that their 
solutions meet payer needs and regulatory expectations, which can help accelerate adoption. However, 
this is dependent on certification requirements being clearly defined, scoped appropriately, and aligned 
to practical implementation realities.  
If ONC were to establish criteria for payer API technology, should CMS require certification to meet 
payer API requirements, or should such certification be made available solely on a voluntary basis? 
Would payers or developers of API technology providing solutions to payers be likely to obtain 
certification on a voluntary basis? 
Mandatory certification would not be the best approach for the industry. The ONC certification program 
has not been fully successful in ensuring APIs function in the real world versus in a testing environment. 
The program adds significant cost to building and maintaining products and may pose challenges for 
new entrants which may unintentionally stifle innovation. Particularly with APIs that include multiple, 
different workflows, rather than just query and retrieve, it is unclear how the ONC certification program 
would be able to certify that they function correctly. We believe that auditing, similar to what CMS NSG 
already performs for HIPAA transactions would be a better path forward for ensuring performance.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** UnitedHealth Group (UHG), signed by the CEO, Optum Insight.
- **Stakeholder type:** Payer / Technology Vendor / Health Services Organization
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** UHG describes UnitedHealthcare as its health benefits business and Optum as its health services business, working with employers, providers, and governments. It also references operational experience implementing ePA, payer APIs, pharmacy infrastructure, clearinghouse connectivity, and cybersecurity controls.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

UHG supports CMS' overall effort to standardize electronic prior authorization for drugs, but urges a nuanced, scalable implementation strategy that preserves existing pharmacy infrastructure and recognizes real-world technology deployment constraints. Its core recommendations are to support unexpired NCPDP standards, permit multi-standard and network-based approaches, extend implementation to up to 24 months after the final rule, retain a uniform March 31 reporting deadline, refine endpoint reporting, and phase any HIPAA FHIR transition without disrupting X12-based workflows.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL/RFI on resiliency and payer APIs.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 91 FR 19890; 42 CFR 423.160; 45 CFR 170.215(a); 45 CFR 162.1301; 45 CFR 162.1201; 45 CFR 170.205(b), 170.205(u), 170.205(c).
- **Standards referenced:** NCPDP SCRIPT, NCPDP Formulary & Benefit, NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit, FHIR, FHIR Endpoint Resource, FHIR APIs, CRD, X12 270/271, X12 278, TEFCA, HIPAA, HITRUST, NIST CSF 2.0, NIST SP 800-63-4, JSON APIs, C-CDA.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: NCPDP standards for pharmacy-benefit drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB are widely adopted, federally mandated under Medicare Part D for their functions, and can reduce burden by creating consistency across plan types.
- **Specific request:** Require impacted payers to support unexpired versions of NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB.

**Topic 2: Multi-standard pathway identification**
- **Provision ID:** MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT / PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** No single tool currently has full visibility into both pharmacy- and medical-benefit coverage. NCPDP F&B/RTPB can provide pharmacy benefit information and may indicate possible medical-benefit coverage, while X12 270/271 guidance may support medical-benefit drug information but not pharmacy benefit data.
- **Specific request:** Permit multi-standard approaches that use existing tools in tandem to determine the appropriate PA pathway.

**Topic 3: Scalable connectivity through TEFCA and existing networks**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** One-to-one FHIR integrations between payers/PBMs and health systems require separate contracting, implementation, testing, and maintenance and may slow adoption.
- **Specific request:** Allow or encourage scalable data exchange for PA through TEFCA, existing NCPDP connectivity, clearinghouses, and network-based approaches rather than relying on point-to-point connections.

**Topic 4: Compliance timeline**
- **Provision ID:** IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE / PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** End-to-end workflow integration across payers, providers, EHRs, pharmacies, PBMs, and trading partners requires coordinated readiness and operationalization, not just deployment.
- **Specific request:** Extend the implementation timeline to up to 24 months after publication of the final rule.

**Topic 5: Public PA metrics deadline**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** State-specific Medicaid/CHIP managed care reporting deadlines would fragment reporting periods, reduce transparency, and make cross-payer comparisons harder.
- **Specific request:** Retain the uniform March 31 annual deadline for all impacted payers.

**Topic 6: Endpoint reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Payer endpoint structures are complex and may vary by plan, product, benefit structure, delegated vendor, service type, and drug pathway.
- **Specific request:** Create a public repository that supports hierarchical mapping of multiple endpoints to a payer entity, plan-level distinctions, and use-case-specific endpoints; pair endpoint transparency with scalable integration strategies.

**Topic 7: HIPAA FHIR prior authorization standards**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** UHG supports FHIR-based workflows but warns that referral transactions are currently processed at scale using X12 278, while FHIR-based referral workflows have not yet been tested at comparable scale.
- **Specific request:** Use pilot testing and phased adoption before changing referral standards; preserve existing transaction frameworks where effective; maintain clear transaction boundaries.

**Topic 8: Eligibility transaction boundaries**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Existing HIPAA eligibility transactions under 45 CFR 162.1201 are intended for eligibility, coverage, and benefits and do not expressly include PA requirements. The intent of an inquiry may be unclear at scheduling or for ancillary services.
- **Specific request:** Clarify boundaries between eligibility and PA discovery, or create a distinct transaction type for determining whether PA is required.

**Topic 9: Later standards versions**
- **Provision ID:** ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Oppose newer-than-proposed NCPDP versions
- **Rationale:** Industry is already mid-transition to the proposed NCPDP versions under Part D deadlines; requiring newer versions would obsolete ongoing implementation work and increase costs.
- **Specific request:** Do not name versions newer than NCPDP SCRIPT 2023011, F&B v60, and RTPB v13 in the final rule.

**Topic 10: Cybersecurity and resiliency RFI**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Cyber threats are increasing, but new mandates should be flexible, risk-based, harmonized, and not duplicative.
- **Specific request:** Reauthorize CISA, establish minimum cyber standards with financial/technical support, harmonize with HIPAA/HITRUST/NIST, embed security-by-design in interoperability, streamline reporting, enforce minimum necessary data sharing, and require provider/delegate identity proofing for ePA.

**Topic 11: Payer API implementation and certification RFI**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI / API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify/Oppose mandatory certification
- **Rationale:** Certification does not guarantee real-world performance, adds cost, and may stifle innovation. FHIR APIs are not plug-and-play, and multiple IG versions create implementation difficulty.
- **Specific request:** Focus on outcomes, data liquidity, existing pharmacy infrastructure, end-to-end interoperability testing, real-world audits, and voluntary or narrowly scoped certification only if CMS proceeds.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S2/S3:** Supports a measured versioning approach and cautions against supporting multiple FHIR IG versions where versions are not backward compatible; recommends coalescing to a single version with adequate adoption time.
- **S12:** Discusses technical challenges for medical-benefit drug PA, particularly need for clinical data at scale and the limitations of point-to-point FHIR connections.
- **S14:** Supports requiring NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB for pharmacy-benefit drugs for Medicaid/CHIP and QHPs.
- **S15:** Responds directly to medical-versus-pharmacy benefit pathway questions by explaining no single tool can definitively identify both pathways and recommending multi-standard approaches.
- **S21:** Recommends an implementation timeline of up to 24 months after final rule publication rather than the proposed October 1, 2027 compliance date.
- **S22:** Notes that newer NCPDP versions would create significant additional development, testing, and deployment costs.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Supports endpoint reporting but asks CMS to account for multiple endpoints, use cases, plan/product distinctions, and real-world integration/security needs.
- **S29/S34/S35:** Recommends retaining a uniform March 31 deadline for PA metrics and Patient Access API usage metrics to preserve comparability.
- **S44:** Supports moving toward FHIR-based prior authorization workflows where they improve efficiency and reduce burden.
- **S45/S46:** Recommends preserving X12-based referral workflows until FHIR referral workflows are pilot-tested and phased in; stresses coexistence and transition planning.
- **S47/S53:** Requests phased adoption and clear transition boundaries for HIPAA standards.
- **S50/S54/S55:** In the payer API RFI, recommends real-world audits and end-to-end testing instead of relying primarily on certification.
- **S60/S61/S63/S65:** Recommends not adopting newer-than-proposed NCPDP versions and coordinating version transitions with current Part D implementation.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to RFIs on resiliency and payer APIs by recommending risk-based cybersecurity, networked exchange, clearinghouse portability, security-by-design, and outcome-based API implementation.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize support for unexpired NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB standards.
2. Permit multi-standard approaches to determine medical- versus pharmacy-benefit PA pathways.
3. Enable scalable PA data exchange through TEFCA, existing NCPDP connectivity, clearinghouses, and health information networks.
4. Extend implementation to up to 24 months after publication of the final rule.
5. Retain the March 31 annual deadline for Medicaid/CHIP managed care PA metrics and Patient Access API usage metrics.
6. Build a hierarchical, flexible public endpoint repository that supports plan-level and use-case-specific endpoint mapping.
7. Phase any HIPAA transition to FHIR-based PA standards and avoid disrupting functioning X12 referral workflows without pilots.
8. Clarify boundaries between eligibility transactions and PA requirement discovery or establish a distinct PA discovery transaction.
9. Do not adopt NCPDP versions newer than SCRIPT 2023011, F&B v60, and RTPB v13.
10. Use voluntary, flexible, risk-based cybersecurity approaches aligned with existing frameworks.
11. Incorporate provider and delegate identity proofing as an ePA API access condition.
12. Use end-to-end real-world interoperability testing and audits rather than mandatory payer API certification.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Fragmented implementation, unrealistic timelines, point-to-point scalability, unclear transaction boundaries, premature standards version changes, duplicative cybersecurity requirements, and certification that fails to reflect real-world performance.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Increased costs, obsolete implementation work, reduced comparability of metrics, security risk from expanded endpoints, disrupted referral workflows, provider confusion, claims submission problems, and delayed adoption.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** One-to-one FHIR connections, multiple endpoint structures, health system contracting/testing burdens, EHR and trading partner readiness, clearinghouse enrollment constraints, multiple FHIR IG versions, vendor capacity, and industry transition to NCPDP Part D standards.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** None as numeric health outcome data in the main proposal section, but the comment cites Part D compliance dates for F&B v60/RTPB v13 (January 1, 2027) and SCRIPT 2023011 (January 1, 2028), and references 72 hours after confirmation as a minimum cyber incident reporting interval.
- **Studies or research referenced:** CAQH CORE 2025 guidance on X12 270/271 for medical-benefit drugs; NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0; NIST SP 800-63-4; Section 405(d) of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015; Cooperative Exchange Trebuchet Pilot Cohort.
- **Examples provided:** Multiple payer endpoints by plan/product/vendor; HETS validation changes increasing provider burden; state Medicaid gateway TPID transfer limitations; point-to-point connection proliferation; clearinghouse-to-clearinghouse FHIR prior authorization pilot.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Payers, PBMs, Medicaid/CHIP programs, QHP issuers, providers, health systems, EHR vendors, clearinghouses, pharmacies, health IT developers, patients, and cybersecurity teams.
- **Economic implications:** UHG warns that newer standards mandates, certification, point-to-point connections, and duplicative reporting could impose significant development, testing, contracting, maintenance, and compliance costs.
- **Technical feasibility:** Mixed; UHG supports the technical direction but stresses that FHIR is not plug-and-play and scalable implementation depends on networks, trading partner readiness, version control, and realistic timelines.
- **Patient care impact:** Potentially positive if ePA reduces time to therapy and provider burden; potentially negative if fragmented or rushed implementation disrupts workflows.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed / Supportive with significant modifications
- **Tone:** Technical, pragmatic, collaborative
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "UHG is supportive of CMS’s continued work on driving toward an interoperable health system, including its current effort to streamline and standardize electronic prior authorization for all drugs." - Context: Opening statement of overall support.
2. "There is no single tool currently available with access to both pharmacy and medical benefit to make the appropriate designation of coverage, but all tools can work in tandem to provide this information." - Context: Recommendation for multi-standard pathway determination.
3. "UHG recommends extending the implementation timeline of up to 24 months following publication of the final rule." - Context: Compliance timeline recommendation.
4. "FHIR APIs are not 'plug and play'." - Context: RFI response on payer API implementation challenges.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - UHG requests up to 24 months after final rule publication and phased HIPAA transition.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment repeatedly cites development, testing, deployment, certification, contracting, and maintenance costs.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - UHG supports ePA to reduce provider burden but warns HETS, point-to-point exchange, and fragmented reporting can increase it.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - The resiliency RFI response emphasizes cybersecurity, identity proofing, minimum necessary data sharing, and avoiding unnecessary exposure of security artifacts.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - The comment focuses heavily on real-world API, network, endpoint, and trading partner feasibility.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - UHG addresses NCPDP version readiness, FHIR IG versioning, and immature FHIR referral workflows.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - UHG supports faster access to medically necessary drugs but frames access as dependent on durable implementation.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment emphasizes coordination among payers, providers, EHRs, PBMs, pharmacies, clearinghouses, ONC, CMS, and HHS.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - UHG directly discusses pathway identification and the lack of a single cross-benefit tool.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports endpoint repositories and comparable metrics while opposing fragmented reporting deadlines.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Strong focus on preserving effective X12, NCPDP, clearinghouse, and pharmacy workflows during transition.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Addresses EHRs, clearinghouses, network intermediaries, health IT developers, and certification burdens.
